text:
Recent work supports testing whether benchmark accuracy actually requires sequence modeling. [Does It Look Sequential? (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.12008) compares original and shuffled interaction sequences across 15 datasets. [Disentangling User and Item Sequence Patterns (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748042) contrasts random shuffling with shuffling constrained by item availability; sequential signals can reflect user behavior, item availability, or both. A [2026 benchmark audit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07125) finds that a simple graph heuristic using only the last one or two interactions competes with sophisticated recommenders, identifying local transition structure and limited long-history dependence as potential shortcuts. Together, these results caution against interpreting high recommendation accuracy as evidence of useful long-range temporal modeling.

A practical synthesis is a paired intervention suite: delete recent, repeated, or distant events and compare each with equal-sized random deletions; permute nonpadding items while preserving counts, including a last-item-fixed permutation. Explicitly control sequence length, padding, and position reassignment so deletion effects are distinguishable from positional artifacts. Validate diagnostic specificity against popularity-only, last-item, and order-insensitive controls: an order probe should remain unchanged for an order-insensitive scorer, and history perturbations should leave a popularity-only scorer unchanged. As a mathematical sanity check, strictly increasing score transformations must preserve HR@10 under consistent tie handling; raw score-distance diagnostics need not remain invariant. These are proposed controls synthesized from the literature, rather than an established standardized suite. Keep validation users and candidates fixed and report paired effects by category. Inference perturbations demonstrate model sensitivity; they cannot by themselves establish causal user intent or latent conformity.
